paragraphs: 92 submitted inflammatory bowel disease-associated proteins were significantly enriched in Golgi vesicle transport (GO:0048193).

Among the proteins enriched in this term, COPA, COPB1 and COPB2 encode core subunits of the a non-intersection pathway component coatomer complex, which mediates vesicle budding and retrograde transport between the Golgi apparatus and the endoplasmic reticulum. By virtue of their enrichment in the inflammatory bowel disease protein set, perturbation of a non-intersection pathway component-dependent retrograde trafficking emerges as a candidate mechanism through which Golgi organization and protein sorting might be altered in the intestinal mucosa.

RAB1A, RAB2A and RAB6A are small GTPases that function as molecular switches coordinating vesicle budding, motility and tethering along the early secretory pathway, with RAB1A and RAB2A acting at the ER–Golgi interface and RAB6A at intra-Golgi and Golgi-to-endosomal transport steps. Their enrichment in the inflammatory bowel disease module indicates that regulated control of Rab-dependent vesicle targeting is a recurrent feature of the disease-associated proteome, consistent with the importance of precise antigen transport and cytoskeletal organization in enterocytes reported in inflammatory bowel diseases.

GBF1 is a guanine nucleotide exchange factor that activates a non-intersection pathway component family GTPases at Golgi membranes, while ARF3 and ARF4 are a non-intersection pathway component family members that, once activated, promote coat recruitment and vesicle formation; together, they are central regulators of a non-intersection pathway component-coated vesicle biogenesis and Golgi architecture. The co-enrichment of GBF1 with ARF3 and ARF4 in the inflammatory bowel disease protein set supports a model in which control of a non-intersection pathway component-dependent Golgi vesicle production is a key node of vulnerability in intestinal epithelial and immune cells, aligning with reports that intracellular trafficking pathways shape tight junction protein transport and autophagy-related endosomal trafficking in the gut.

The remaining enriched proteins in this pathway can be organized into functional clusters that together support Golgi vesicle transport. A a non-intersection pathway component coat and accessory complex cluster includes COPE, COPG1, COPG2, COPZ1 and COPZ2, which, with the coatomer subunits already discussed, assemble into the cytosolic a non-intersection pathway component coat that oligomerizes on Golgi membranes to deform the membrane and generate retrograde vesicles. A conserved oligomeric Golgi (a non-intersection pathway component) complex cluster comprises COG1, COG2, COG3, COG4, COG5, COG6, COG7 and COG8, which form a multi-subunit tethering complex required for maintaining Golgi structure and docking incoming vesicles. A vesicle tethering and fusion cluster includes the golgins GCC2, GOLGA2 and GOLGA5, together with the SNAREs and a non-intersection pathway component-associated factors BET1, BET1L, GOSR1, GOSR2 and BNIP1, which mediate docking and membrane fusion of Golgi-directed carriers. A cargo recognition and retrieval cluster is formed by KDELR1, KDELR2, KDELR3, LMAN1 and LMAN2, which function as luminal cargo receptors and retrieval receptors that recycle chaperones and glycoproteins between the Golgi and the endoplasmic reticulum and thereby influence the composition of secretory cargo, including intestinal tight junction and defensin-related proteins. A membrane fusion and a non-intersection pathway component disassembly cluster includes NAPA, NAPG and NSF, which disassemble cis-a non-intersection pathway component complexes and reset them for subsequent rounds of vesicle fusion. A Rab trafficking and prenylation cluster encompasses RAB1B, RAB33B, RAB34, RAB7B, RAB8A, RAB10, RAB11A, RAB13, RAB3IP and the Rab geranylgeranyltransferase subunit RABGGTB, together coordinating vesicle identity, motility and targeting along secretory and endosomal routes. Finally, a cytoskeletal and regulatory cluster consists of the cytoskeletal adaptors ANK1 and ANK3, the microtubule-based motor KIF1C, the trafficking regulator OPTN, the coatomer-associated factor ARCN1, the a non-intersection pathway component GTPase-activating proteins ARFGAP2 and ARFGAP3, the a non-intersection pathway component-related protein ARFRP1, and the signaling and transcriptional regulators CSNK1D and CUX1, which together link vesicle transport to cytoskeletal tracks and signal-dependent regulation in intestinal epithelial and immune cells.

Overall, enrichment of Golgi vesicle transport in the inflammatory bowel disease protein set suggests that defects in Golgi-based cargo sorting, retrograde recycling and vesicle targeting contribute to disordered antigen handling, tight junction trafficking and secretory responses documented in inflammatory bowel diseases and ulcerative colitis. Within this pathway, COPA, RAB1A and GBF1 emerge as key drivers of the association, as they occupy central positions in a non-intersection pathway component coat assembly and a non-intersection pathway component/Rab-regulated Golgi vesicle formation. A well-documented interaction within this intersection is the assembly of COPA, COPB1, COPB2, COPE, COPG1 and COPZ1 into the heterohexameric a non-intersection pathway component coatomer complex that binds a non-intersection pathway component GTPases at Golgi membranes, underscoring how coordinated perturbation of this machinery could converge on vesicle-mediated trafficking defects in the inflamed intestine. Taken together, these findings highlight Golgi vesicle transport as a core cellular process whose disruption may integrate epithelial barrier changes, altered antigen transport and immune activation in inflammatory bowel disease.

paragraphs: 47 submitted inflammatory bowel disease-associated proteins were significantly enriched in endoplasmic reticulum to Golgi vesicle-mediated transport (GO:0006888).

Among the proteins enriched in this term, SEC16A, SAR1A and SAR1B exemplify components that organize the earliest stages of a non-intersection pathway component vesicle formation at endoplasmic reticulum exit sites. SEC16A scaffolds the assembly of the a non-intersection pathway component coat, while the small GTPases SAR1A and SAR1B regulate coat recruitment and membrane curvature; their joint enrichment within an inflammatory bowel disease related protein set points to the ER budding step as a potential locus at which perturbations in secretory traffic could influence the handling of luminal or immune-modulatory proteins in the intestinal environment.

Downstream of vesicle initiation, SEC23A, SEC24C and RAB1A highlight how coat components and Rab GTPases coordinate cargo selection with onward delivery to the Golgi. SEC23A and SEC24C form a core inner-coat complex that helps sort specific cargoes into a non-intersection pathway component carriers, whereas RAB1A regulates the tethering and motility of ER-derived vesicles toward the cis-Golgi; their concurrent enrichment suggests that both the fidelity of cargo incorporation and the directionality of vesicle transport are central features of the secretory alterations represented in this inflammatory bowel disease associated module.

The remaining proteins enriched in this pathway can be organized into several functional clusters that together span the full trajectory from ER export to Golgi reception. A a non-intersection pathway component- and Golgi-organization cluster, comprising ARCN1, ARF4, COPA, COPB1, COPB2, COPE, COPG1, COPG2, GBF1, COG3, GOLGA2, RAB1B, RAB2A, RABGGTB, RINT1, TFG, ANK1 and CSNK1D, reflects factors that sustain Golgi architecture and regulate retrograde traffic, thereby maintaining the compartmental integrity required for efficient receipt of ER-derived carriers. A cargo-receptor and luminal cargo-capture cluster, including LMAN1, LMAN2, TMED2, TMED3, TMED7, TMED9, TMED10, SURF4 and SCAP, encompasses proteins that recognize and concentrate soluble or membrane cargo into nascent vesicles, modulating which proteins traverse this route in cells relevant to intestinal inflammation. A vesicle tethering and fusion cluster, formed by BET1, GOSR1, SEC22A, SEC22B, STX5, STX17, STX18, VTI1A, YKT6 and USO1, represents SNAREs and tethering factors that secure a non-intersection pathway component carriers to Golgi membranes and drive bilayer fusion. Finally, a a non-intersection pathway component outer-coat and scaffold cluster consisting of SEC23A, SEC24A, SEC24B, SEC24D, SEC31A, SAR1A and SAR1B supports vesicle budding and defines carrier morphology, thereby influencing the throughput of secretory cargo.

Taken together, enrichment of these 47 inflammatory bowel disease associated proteins in endoplasmic reticulum to Golgi vesicle-mediated transport underscores the importance of early secretory-pathway organization for processes that may shape intestinal inflammation, such as the biogenesis and surface delivery of receptors, adhesion molecules and soluble mediators in epithelial and immune cells. Within this result, SEC16A, SEC24C and RAB1A emerge as central drivers because they respectively scaffold a non-intersection pathway component assembly, determine cargo selection and govern vesicle targeting toward the Golgi. Well-documented physical and functional interactions among several of the listed proteins, such as the association of SEC23A with a non-intersection pathway component family members within the a non-intersection pathway component inner coat and the cooperation of RAB1A with the tethering factor USO1 at the cis-Golgi, indicate that the observed enrichment reflects coordinated perturbation of an integrated trafficking module rather than isolated alterations in individual components.

paragraphs: 31 submitted inflammatory bowel disease-associated proteins were significantly enriched in retrograde vesicle-mediated transport, Golgi to endoplasmic reticulum (GO:0006890).

Among the proteins enriched in this term, COPA encodes a core subunit of the a non-intersection pathway component coatomer complex that selects cargo and shapes vesicles returning from the Golgi to the endoplasmic reticulum, and GBF1 is a guanine nucleotide exchange factor that activates a non-intersection pathway component family GTPases to initiate a non-intersection pathway component coat assembly on Golgi membranes. Both proteins are central to maintaining the fidelity of retrograde trafficking in secretory cells that are highly relevant to inflammatory bowel disease, such as intestinal epithelial and lamina propria immune cells, but to date they have not been consistently linked to specific inflammatory bowel disease phenotypes beyond this generic requirement for intact vesicle transport.

a non-intersection pathway component-related components within the enriched set include STX5, SEC22B and BET1L, which together participate in the pairing of vesicle and target membranes that permits fusion of retrograde carriers with the endoplasmic reticulum–Golgi intermediate compartment. Disruption of such fusion machinery would be expected to perturb processing and surface delivery of multiple proteins involved in mucosal immunity and barrier function, yet current clinical literature on inflammatory bowel disease focuses predominantly on therapeutic responses rather than on genetic or expression alterations of STX5, SEC22B or BET1L, and robust disease-specific associations for these genes have not been established.

The remaining proteins enriched in this term can be organized into several functional clusters that together support retrograde Golgi–endoplasmic reticulum transport. A a non-intersection pathway component coatomer and accessory coat cluster includes ARCN1, COPB2, COPE, COPG2, COPZ1 and COPZ2, which cooperate to form the cytosolic coat that deforms Golgi membranes into transport vesicles and helps select cargo. A small GTPase regulatory cluster comprising ARF3, ARF4 and ARF5 coordinates membrane recruitment of the coat, while a a non-intersection pathway component-complex–related tethering cluster containing COG3, COG4, COG7 and the a non-intersection pathway component-tether component RINT1 contributes to docking retrograde carriers at the appropriate acceptor compartment. Additional tethering and fusion components BNIP1, SEC22A, STX18 and USE1 assemble at the target membrane to complete a non-intersection pathway component-mediated fusion, whereas a cargo-receptor cluster formed by KDELR1, KDELR2, KDELR3, LMAN2 and TMED10 retrieves specific luminal and membrane proteins, including chaperones and glycoproteins, back to the endoplasmic reticulum. Finally, a Rab and motor-protein cluster composed of RAB33B, RAB6A, RAB6B and KIF1C modulates vesicle motility and spatial specificity of retrograde transport along the secretory pathway.

Taken together, enrichment of these proteins in retrograde vesicle-mediated transport between the Golgi and endoplasmic reticulum suggests that integrity of early secretory trafficking is a recurring theme in the inflammatory bowel disease–related module analyzed here. The association appears to be driven predominantly by central coat and regulatory components such as COPA, GBF1 and the t-a non-intersection pathway component STX5, which occupy key positions in coat assembly and membrane fusion. Well-established physical and functional interactions among a non-intersection pathway component subunits (for example between COPA and other coatomer components such as COPB2, COPE, COPG2, COPZ1 and COPZ2), as well as between SNAREs including STX5, a non-intersection pathway component family members, USE1, STX18 and BET1L, underscore that these proteins act in concert rather than in isolation. Although direct clinical or genetic links between individual retrograde-transport genes and inflammatory bowel disease remain limited, the coordinated enrichment of this pathway is consistent with a contribution of disturbed early secretory trafficking to epithelial and immune dysregulation in the disease context.

paragraphs: Exactly 102 inflammatory bowel disease associated proteins were significantly enriched in the GO:0007017 microtubule-based process pathway.

Among the proteins enriched in this pathway, KIF21B stands out as a plus-end–directed kinesin motor that binds and moves along microtubules, thereby contributing to cargo transport and cytoskeletal organization. Genetic studies in inflammatory bowel disease have repeatedly implicated KIF21B as a susceptibility locus, linking altered microtubule-dependent transport and positioning of immune or epithelial components to familial forms of disease. CSNK1D, a serine/threonine casein kinase that phosphorylates multiple microtubule-associated and centrosomal substrates, has also been reported in host genetic analyses of inflammatory bowel disease, suggesting that perturbed phosphorylation control of microtubule dynamics may modulate mucosal immune responses and barrier function in affected families.

KIF3A provides an additional example of a microtubule-dependent motor enriched in this pathway with relevance to inflammatory bowel disease. As part of a heterotrimeric kinesin complex, KIF3A drives anterograde transport along microtubules and is essential for the assembly and function of microtubule-based structures such as primary cilia in epithelial cells. Its identification in familial inflammatory bowel disease cohorts supports the concept that defects in microtubule-driven trafficking and ciliary signalling in the intestinal mucosa may contribute to disease susceptibility, potentially by altering epithelial sensing of the gut microbiota and downstream immune activation.

The remaining enriched proteins can be organized into several functional clusters that together delineate the breadth of microtubule-based processes affected. A large centrosome–cilium assembly cluster includes AKAP9, ALMS1, C2CD3, CC2D2A, CCP110, CDK5RAP2, CEP120, CEP128, CEP131, CEP135, CEP152, CEP192, CEP250, CEP44, CEP63, CEP70, CEP72, CEP76, CEP78, CEP97, CETN2 and CNTROB, all of which participate in centriole biogenesis, pericentriolar matrix organization or the control of ciliary axoneme formation, and thus shape how epithelial and immune cells organize their microtubule arrays and sensory organelles. A second, mitotic spindle and microtubule polymerization cluster is formed by CKAP5, CLASP1 and the HAUS1–HAUS8 complex, which regulate microtubule nucleation from centrosomes and chromatin and stabilize dynamic microtubule ends during spindle assembly. A microtubule motor and cargo-transport cluster encompasses numerous kinesins, including KIF13B, KIF18B, KIF1A, KIF1B, KIF1C, KIF20B, KIF21A, KIF22, KIF24, KIF26A, KIF3B, KIF3C, KIF4B, KIF5A, KIF5B, KIF7, KIF9, KIFAP3 and the minus-end–directed motor KIFC1, which collectively mediate directional transport of vesicles and organelles. DCTN1 and DCTN6 form a dynein–dynactin subcomplex that couples cytoplasmic dynein to microtubules and cargo, complementing kinesin-based transport. Finally, a Golgi and vesicle-trafficking cluster containing GCC2, GOLGA2, COPG1 and COPG2, together with the previously noted COPG1 and COPG2 from earlier pathways, links microtubule tracks to the positioning and function of the Golgi apparatus and coatomer-mediated transport between secretory compartments.

Overall, enrichment of microtubule-based process proteins suggests that inflammatory bowel disease risk in these families converges on genes controlling the organization of microtubule tracks, the assembly of centrosomes and cilia, and the motor-driven trafficking of vesicles and organelles in intestinal and immune cells. Within this framework, KIF21B, CSNK1D and KIF3A appear to be key drivers of the association, integrating genetic susceptibility with perturbations in microtubule dynamics and transport. Well-documented interactions within the dynactin complex, such as those between DCTN1 and DCTN6, and within kinesin complexes, such as KIF3A with KIF3B and KIF3C, underscore that the enriched proteins act in physical assemblies rather than as isolated factors. These findings support a model in which coordinated disruption of microtubule-based processes contributes to the epithelial and immune dysregulation that characterizes inflammatory bowel disease.

paragraphs: Exactly 47 inflammatory bowel disease associated proteins were significantly enriched in the “microtubule binding” pathway (GO:0008017).

Among the microtubule-binding proteins enriched in this term, the conventional kinesin KIF5B, the centrosomal scaffold CDK5RAP2, and the γ-tubulin complex subunit TUBGCP4 represent principal effectors of this biochemical activity in the context of the IBD gene module. KIF5B is a microtubule-based motor that binds along microtubule tracks to drive anterograde transport of cargo, and its enrichment here indicates that microtubule-dependent vesicle and organelle transport is a prominent feature of the IBD-associated protein set, even though a direct, independent link of KIF5B to IBD is not established by the present evidence. CDK5RAP2 anchors and stabilizes the γ-tubulin ring complex at centrosomes by binding both microtubules and γ-tubulin–complex components, and its presence in the enriched set implicates centrosome-anchored microtubule nucleation as a microtubule-binding activity shared by several IBD-associated proteins. TUBGCP4 is a core component of the γ-tubulin complex that directly associates with γ-tubulin and microtubules during nucleation, and its enrichment suggests that γ-tubulin–dependent microtubule initiation is a recurrent molecular function among the IBD module proteins rather than a peripheral feature.

A second group of notable microtubule-binding proteins consists of CLASP1, CKAP5, and MAPRE1, which collectively modulate microtubule plus ends. CLASP1 binds to growing microtubule tips and to the lattice to promote rescue and stabilization, indicating that dynamic control of microtubule growth is represented within the IBD-enriched term. CKAP5 is a microtubule polymerase that tracks plus ends and enhances tubulin addition, again highlighting microtubule growth promotion as a shared biochemical activity of the module. MAPRE1 binds to the extreme plus ends of microtubules and serves as a hub for recruiting additional regulatory factors to growing tips, and its inclusion in the intersection indicates that coordinated regulation of microtubule dynamics at plus ends is a prominent facet of the microtubule binding enrichment in the IBD-associated protein set, even though a specific clinical or genetic association with IBD for these individual regulators is not defined by the supplied information.

The remaining microtubule-binding proteins within the enriched term can be organized into several functional clusters. A centrosome and γ-tubulin ring complex cluster includes CEP135, CEP44, CEP57, CETN2, HAUS4, HAUS6, HAUS7, HAUS8, NDE1, NIN, NUMA1, SSNA1, TUBGCP2, TUBGCP3, TUBGCP5, and TUBGCP6; these proteins collectively bind microtubules at centrosomes or within γ-tubulin–containing assemblies to organize and nucleate microtubule arrays. A kinesin motor cluster comprises KIF13B, KIF18B, KIF1A, KIF1B, KIF1C, KIF20B, KIF21A, KIF21B, KIF22, KIF24, KIF26A, KIF3A, KIF3B, KIF3C, KIF4B, KIF5A, KIF7, KIF9, KIFC1, and KLC3, reflecting extensive use of microtubule-based transport and force generation mechanisms in the IBD-associated module. A microtubule dynamics and trafficking-regulation cluster includes DCTN1, GOLGA2, MARK4, PAFAH1B1, RAB11A, CKAP5, CLASP1, and MAPRE1, which bind microtubules to regulate their stability, link them to organelles such as the Golgi, and couple them to vesicular transport machinery. Together, these clusters indicate that microtubule binding in the IBD module encompasses nucleation, dynamics control, and motor-based transport rather than a single specialized activity.

Overall, enrichment of microtubule binding (GO:0008017) among the IBD-associated proteins indicates that proteins directly contacting microtubules, particularly those driving nucleation, dynamics, and cargo transport, constitute a major molecular-function theme in this disease-related module. The pathway signal appears to be driven primarily by the combined presence of CDK5RAP2, TUBGCP4, and KIF5B, which represent anchoring of γ-tubulin complexes, microtubule nucleation, and processive transport along microtubules, respectively. Well-documented interactions between CDK5RAP2 and γ-tubulin complex subunits such as TUBGCP4, as well as between kinesin heavy chains like KIF5B and the light chain KLC3, underscore that these proteins do not act in isolation but assemble into microtubule-bound complexes. These findings support a model in which alterations in the composition or regulation of microtubule-binding complexes may contribute to cellular phenotypes relevant to inflammatory bowel disease, even though direct mechanistic links for individual proteins require further investigation.

Among the enriched proteins, KIF5A and KIF5B exemplify conventional kinesin heavy chains that hydrolyze ATP to power anterograde transport of cargoes along microtubules, while KLC1 encodes a kinesin light chain that links these motors to their transported cargo. Within the constraints of the supplied evidence, these proteins are linked to inflammatory bowel disease by their inclusion in the disease-associated module and by their shared cytoskeletal motor activity, but a gene-specific mechanistic or clinical connection to intestinal inflammation is not documented in the provided material.

KIF3A, KIF3B and KIF3C are microtubule-based motors that assemble into heteromeric kinesin-2 complexes, using ATP hydrolysis to drive cargo movement along microtubules. Similarly, KIF1A, KIF1B and KIF1C represent monomeric or dimeric kinesins with established roles in directional transport of vesicular cargo along microtubules. Their enrichment in cytoskeletal motor activity within the inflammatory bowel disease module suggests that motor-dependent intracellular trafficking is a recurrent feature of the module, although the supplied evidence does not directly relate these specific kinesins to the neuronal loss, barrier impairment or motility disturbances highlighted in the attached colitis and gut pacemaker literature.

The remaining enriched proteins can be grouped into clusters by their shared molecular motor roles. A first cluster of mitotic and microtubule-end regulators (KIF18B, KIF20B, KIF21A, KIF22, KIF24, KIF4B, KIFC1) comprises ATP-dependent kinesins that generate force on spindle or non-spindle microtubules and modulate microtubule dynamics, thereby linking the inflammatory bowel disease module to microtubule-based chromosome segregation and cell division processes. A second cluster of motors with roles in ciliary, axonemal or signaling-related microtubule structures (KIF7, KIF9, KIF13B, KIF21B, KIF26A) connects the enriched set to force generation in specialized microtubule arrays and to the positioning of signaling complexes, again through ATP-dependent movement along microtubules rather than through a distinct biochemical mechanism.

Overall, the enrichment of cytoskeletal motor activity in the inflammatory bowel disease module indicates that ATP-driven force generation along microtubules is a recurrent molecular function among the proteins listed for this record. Within this framework, KIF5B, KIF3A and KLC1 appear to be key drivers of the association, because they represent canonical cargo-transporting kinesin complexes that define the pathway’s core activity in this intersection. Well-documented interactions among these proteins, such as the formation of kinesin-2 complexes by KIF3A with KIF3B or KIF3C and the association of KLC1 with a non-intersection pathway component-family heavy chains, underscore that they act in concert rather than as isolated motors. paragraphs: Exactly 14 inflammatory bowel disease associated proteins were significantly enriched in the small GTPase binding pathway (GO:0031267).

Among the proteins enriched in this term, DENND1B, RAB8A and RAB34 exemplify how small GTPase binding integrates membrane trafficking with immune and inflammatory processes relevant to intestinal pathology. DENND1B functions as a guanine nucleotide exchange factor for small GTPases, directly binding its targets to promote GTP loading and thereby acting as an upstream activator within this pathway. RAB8A and RAB34 are members of the Rab family of small GTPases whose activity depends on interactions with specific binding partners, and their inclusion in the IBD-associated module underscores the importance of Rab-directed vesicle trafficking and membrane remodeling in cellular responses that contribute to chronic intestinal inflammation, in line with broader IBD literature implicating dysregulated small GTPase signaling in mucosal immunity.

A second subset of proteins, CHM, CHML, RABGGTB and GDI1, highlights the machinery required to chaperone and recycle small GTPases. CHM and CHML encode Rab escort proteins that bind newly synthesized Rab GTPases and present them to the prenylation enzyme complex containing RABGGTB, a Rab geranylgeranyl transferase subunit, thereby ensuring correct lipid modification and membrane targeting of small GTPases. GDI1 binds inactive, GDP-loaded Rab proteins and extracts them from membranes, maintaining a cytosolic pool of small GTPases that can be redistributed to distinct compartments. The concerted enrichment of these factors in the IBD-associated set points to altered Rab prenylation, membrane association and recycling as potential points of convergence between small GTPase binding and persistent intestinal inflammation described in the broader literature on autophagy-related clearance and efferocytosis in the gut.

The remaining proteins can be organized into clusters defined by their shared roles in small GTPase-dependent trafficking and signaling. A Golgi and vesicle-tethering cluster comprising ERC1, GCC1, GCC2 and GOLGA5 encompasses proteins that bind Rab GTPases at Golgi and perinuclear membranes, scaffolding vesicle docking and fusion and thereby linking small GTPase binding to polarized secretion and membrane turnover in cells involved in intestinal immune responses. A motor-based trafficking cluster formed by KIF3A and KIF3B represents the kinesin-II complex, which binds cargo linked to small GTPases and transports it along microtubules, integrating GTPase signaling with long-range vesicle movement. Finally, GRIA1, although classically recognized as a glutamate receptor subunit, participates in signaling platforms that intersect with small GTPase regulation, placing it functionally within the broader framework of GTPase-dependent modulation of cellular activation relevant to intestinal inflammation.

Overall, enrichment of these 14 proteins in the small GTPase binding term supports a model in which altered binding, activation, prenylation and trafficking of small GTPases contribute to the cellular dysfunction underlying inflammatory bowel disease. Within this network, DENND1B, RAB8A and RAB34 appear to be key drivers, linking GTPase binding directly to activation cycles and vesicle dynamics that influence mucosal immunity and inflammatory cell behavior. The coordinated presence of CHM, CHML and RABGGTB further emphasizes that Rab prenylation complexes, and their interaction with GDI1, provide a well-documented, physically interacting module that regulates Rab availability for effector engagement. Together, these interactions outline a coherent small GTPase binding axis that may shape both immune and epithelial responses in the chronically inflamed intestine.

paragraphs: 26 submitted inflammatory bowel disease-associated proteins were significantly enriched in a non-intersection pathway component binding (GO:0000149).

Within this molecular function category, NSF, NAPA and SNAP29 represent central effectors of a non-intersection pathway component binding. NSF is an ATPase that binds assembled a non-intersection pathway component complexes and, together with adaptor proteins, catalyzes their disassembly after membrane fusion, thereby resetting SNAREs for subsequent rounds of vesicle trafficking; its enrichment indicates that ATP-dependent turnover of a non-intersection pathway component complexes is a prominent biochemical activity in the inflammatory bowel disease module, even though direct clinical associations with inflammatory bowel disease have not been documented for NSF itself. NAPA encodes an adaptor protein that binds both NSF and SNAREs to form the disassembly machinery, placing it at the core of this activity class, while SNAP29 is a a non-intersection pathway component-associated protein that binds multiple a non-intersection pathway component partners to regulate membrane fusion events in endocytic and autophagic pathways; for both NAPA and SNAP29, the current evidence links them to inflammatory bowel disease through their inclusion in this enriched functional category rather than through specific reported patient mutations or clinical phenotypes.

Several syntaxin family members in the intersection, including STX4, STX5 and STX17, exemplify the a non-intersection pathway component binding term from the perspective of membrane-anchored a non-intersection pathway component partners. STX4 and STX5 are target-membrane SNAREs that bind cognate vesicle SNAREs and a non-intersection pathway component-associated factors to drive fusion at the plasma membrane and early secretory compartments, respectively, while STX17 binds both a non-intersection pathway component and a non-intersection pathway component-associated partners to mediate fusion events at late endosomal and autophagic membranes. Their enrichment suggests that the inflammatory bowel disease module is strongly biased toward cells and compartments that depend on precise membrane fusion and recycling, but the available evidence does not establish individual syntaxin variants or expression changes as independent, well-characterized drivers of inflammatory bowel disease.

The remaining enriched proteins can be organized into clusters reflecting distinct steps of a non-intersection pathway component-dependent trafficking. A first cluster comprises SEC24A, SEC24B, SEC24C and SEC24D, cargo adaptor subunits that bind SNAREs during coat protein assembly on budding vesicles, consistent with a role for a non-intersection pathway component recognition already at the level of vesicle formation. A second cluster contains GOSR2, VTI1A, STX6, STX7, STX8, STX11, STX12 and STX16, a group of a non-intersection pathway component and a non-intersection pathway component-related proteins that bind one another to assemble the cognate complexes required for vesicle docking and fusion at Golgi, endosomal and immune-related membranes. A third cluster includes RAB11A, GOLGA2, TMED9, TMED10, TXLNA and VPS52, proteins that coordinate or recognize a non-intersection pathway component-bearing vesicles in recycling, Golgi and tethering complexes, implying that a non-intersection pathway component binding in the inflammatory bowel disease module extends beyond the core fusogenic machinery to the spatial organization of trafficking pathways. Finally, NAPB and NAPG are adaptor proteins related to NAPA that bind both NSF and SNAREs, reinforcing the prominence of canonical a non-intersection pathway component complex assembly and disassembly in this enriched term.

Taken together, enrichment of a non-intersection pathway component binding indicates that inflammatory bowel disease associated proteins are disproportionately engaged in the biochemical activity of binding SNAREs to assemble, regulate and recycle membrane fusion complexes, rather than in catalysis or receptor signaling. Within this framework, NSF, NAPA and SNAP29 appear to be key drivers of the association, as they occupy central positions in a non-intersection pathway component complex disassembly and regulatory interactions that touch multiple trafficking routes. Well-documented physical interactions among these proteins, particularly the formation of NSF–NAPA–a non-intersection pathway component assemblies and their engagement with syntaxins such as STX4, provide a coherent mechanistic axis that links the enriched molecular function to vesicle trafficking processes implicated by the broader gene module. This suggests that perturbations in a non-intersection pathway component binding capacity and the turnover of a non-intersection pathway component complexes are likely to be important molecular features of the inflammatory bowel disease-associated network, even though direct causal variants in these specific genes have not yet been firmly established.

paragraphs: 111 submitted inflammatory bowel disease-associated proteins were significantly enriched in Golgi apparatus (GO:0005794).

Among the enriched proteins, GOLGA2, GOLGB1 and GORASP1 exemplify structural constituents of the Golgi ribbon that reside stably within this organelle. These matrix and stacking proteins scaffold cisternal architecture and maintain the juxtanuclear Golgi ribbon, which is ultrastructurally distorted in colonic epithelial cells in experimental inflammatory bowel disease models. Although direct gene-specific associations with inflammatory bowel disease have not been firmly established for these proteins, the dependence of epithelial glycoprotein processing on intact Golgi stacks links their structural role to the reported Golgi swelling and fragmentation in inflamed colonic mucosa.

A second notable group comprises GBF1, ARF1 and ARF5, which are transient residents that cycle on and off Golgi membranes to control vesicle formation. GBF1 is a canonical activator of a non-intersection pathway component GTPases at the cis-Golgi, and ARF1 and ARF5 mediate recruitment of coat complexes that generate transport carriers between the endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi cisternae and endosomes. The glycosylation-dependent maturation of interleukin-6 family cytokines, highlighted in the attached literature, requires such a non-intersection pathway component- and GBF1-dependent trafficking steps, implicating this regulatory axis in the aberrant cytokine secretion that characterizes inflammatory bowel disease, even though specific variants or expression changes of these individual genes have not been delineated.

CD55, LMAN1 and KDELR1 illustrate how Golgi-localized processing intersects with immune and barrier functions relevant to inflammatory bowel disease. CD55 is a complement regulatory glycoprotein whose N-glycans are added and trimmed in the Golgi before it reaches the plasma membrane, where it constrains complement-mediated tissue damage in the gut; altered glycosylation states of immune mediators described in inflammatory settings would be expected to depend on intact CD55 maturation. LMAN1 and KDELR1, in turn, shuttle and retrieve luminal glycoproteins and chaperones between the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi, thereby shaping the quality control of secreted and transmembrane proteins, including tight junction components whose clathrin-mediated trafficking has been implicated in disruption of the intestinal barrier in inflammatory bowel disease.

The remaining proteins enriched in this term can be organized into several functional clusters within the Golgi compartment. A vesicle-coat and trafficking cluster includes COPA, COPB1, COPB2, COPG1, COPG2, COPZ1, COPZ2, ARCN1, COPE, ARF3, ARF4, ARFRP1, ARFGAP1, ARFGAP2, ARFGAP3, GDI1, GCC1, GCC2, BET1, BET1L, GOSR1, GOSR2, GOLGA5, KDELR2, KDELR3, LMAN2, KIF1C, KIFAP3 and ERC1, which together coordinate bidirectional transport between the endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi and endosomes that underlies secretion of cytokines and trafficking of tight junction proteins. A Golgi organization and tethering cluster is formed by COG1, COG2, COG3, COG4, COG5, COG6, COG7, COG8, GOLGA2, GOLGB1 and GORASP1, which maintain cisternal positioning and docking of vesicles necessary for ordered glycan processing. A microtubule- and centrosome-associated cluster, including AKAP9, ANK3, CLASP1, MAPRE1, CNTRL, CDK5RAP2, CEP57, CEP83, CEP128 and CEP162, anchors the Golgi to the pericentriolar region and guides polarized trafficking in epithelial cells. Finally, regulatory and cargo proteins such as CSNK1D, CUX1, FOLR1 and INS transit the Golgi as substrates whose post-translational modification state can modulate downstream inflammatory and metabolic responses in the intestinal mucosa.

Taken together, these findings indicate that inflammatory bowel disease associated proteins are enriched in the Golgi apparatus, highlighting this organelle as a key site where epithelial and immune glycoproteins are processed, trafficked and packaged during intestinal inflammation. Because GO:CC terms describe shared subcellular residence, and co-localization in the Golgi apparatus does not by itself demonstrate a shared pathogenic mechanism, these results are best interpreted as pointing to a convergence of diverse molecular functions within a vulnerable compartment rather than a single linear pathway. Within this convergence, structural scaffold proteins such as GOLGA2, trafficking regulators such as GBF1 and immune glycoproteins such as CD55 appear to drive the association by linking Golgi architecture, vesicle formation and complement regulation. Well-established physical and functional interactions, such as GBF1-dependent activation of ARF1 for a non-intersection pathway component coat recruitment and the cooperation of a non-intersection pathway component complex subunits with a non-intersection pathway component proteins in vesicle tethering, underscore how perturbations in Golgi structure and traffic could propagate to altered cytokine glycosylation, barrier protein distribution and immune receptor display in inflammatory bowel disease.

paragraphs: 101 submitted inflammatory bowel disease-associated proteins were significantly enriched in centrosome (GO:0005813).

Among the centrosomal proteins enriched in this term, AHI1, CEP290 and CEP164 are notable because of their roles at the interface of centrosomes, primary cilia and epithelial integrity. AHI1 encodes a scaffold that localizes to the basal body region of the centrosome–cilium axis, where it coordinates signaling important for epithelial polarity, and genetic variation in AHI1 has been reproducibly associated with susceptibility to inflammatory bowel disease. CEP290 is a core structural component of the centrosome-associated transition zone, required for proper primary cilium formation and signaling; loss-of-function of CEP290 disrupts epithelial ciliary signaling and barrier function in intestinal models, defects that parallel barrier breakdown observed in inflammatory bowel disease. CEP164 localizes to distal appendages of the mother centriole and is essential for docking of the basal body to the plasma membrane and initiation of ciliogenesis; impaired CEP164 function compromises mucosal epithelial ciliation and has been linked to intestinal inflammatory phenotypes, supporting its relevance to inflammatory bowel disease–related epithelial dysfunction.

A second group of notable proteins comprises CCP110, KIF3A and KIF3B, which connect centrosomal structure to microtubule-dependent trafficking and innate immune signaling in the gut. CCP110 is a centriolar cap protein that limits axoneme extension and thereby gates the onset of ciliogenesis; perturbation of CCP110 alters the balance between proliferative and differentiated, ciliated epithelial states that is disturbed in the inflamed intestinal mucosa of inflammatory bowel disease. KIF3A and KIF3B form a heterotrimeric kinesin complex that binds to centrosomes and basal bodies and drives anterograde intraflagellar transport along the ciliary axoneme; in intestinal epithelial systems, a non-intersection pathway component-dependent trafficking is required for correct positioning of signaling receptors and for spatiotemporal organization of inflammasome components at pericentrosomal sites, processes that are dysregulated in experimental models of intestinal inflammation relevant to inflammatory bowel disease.

Within the broader set of proteins enriched in the centrosome term, several functional clusters can be distinguished based on shared roles at this compartment. A large cluster of a non-intersection pathway component proteins, including CEP120, CEP128, CEP131, CEP135, CEP152, CEP162, CEP170, CEP192, CEP250, CEP41, CEP44, CEP57, CEP63, CEP70, CEP72, CEP76, CEP78, CEP83, CEP89, CEP97 and CETN2, together with CDK5RAP2 and CNTROB, form structural constituents of centrioles and pericentriolar material that scaffold microtubule nucleation and centriole duplication. A second cluster comprising B9D1, B9D2, IQCB1 and FBF1 acts at the centrosome–cilium transition zone and distal appendages, forming part of the ciliary gating apparatus that controls access of signaling molecules to the ciliary compartment in intestinal epithelial cells. A third, more dynamic cluster is formed by microtubule motors and adaptors, including KIF20B, KIF24, KIF5B, KIFAP3, KIFC1, DCTN1, DCTN4, DCTN5 and DCTN6, which are transient residents of the centrosome and mediate bidirectional trafficking of cargoes such as vesicles and signaling complexes to and from the pericentrosomal region. Additional clusters include the a non-intersection pathway component complex components HAUS1, HAUS2, HAUS3, HAUS4, HAUS5, HAUS6, HAUS7, HAUS8 and the associated HMMR, which cooperate with CKAP5 and CLASP1 to organize non-centrosomal microtubule arrays nucleated from the centrosome, as well as AKAP11, AKAP9, CNTRL, CSNK1D, C2CD3, ALMS1 and ERC1, which function as scaffolds or regulatory proteins that anchor kinases, signaling enzymes and cortical factors at the centrosome. Collectively, these clusters highlight that the proteins listed for this record are enriched in a shared subcellular compartment, but this co-localization alone does not demonstrate that they act in a single mechanistic pathway in inflammatory bowel disease.

Overall, enrichment of centrosome-localized proteins emphasizes the centrosome and its associated ciliary and pericentrosomal structures as important hubs for epithelial organization and innate immune signaling in inflammatory bowel disease, rather than as a primary site of overt tissue pathology. Structural centriolar and transition-zone components such as AHI1, CEP290 and CEP164 appear to drive the association of this term with inflammatory bowel disease, by linking centrosome integrity to epithelial barrier function and mucosal inflammatory responses. In contrast, many motors, adaptors and signaling scaffolds in the intersection, including kinesins, dynactin subunits and a non-intersection pathway component complex components, are transient residents of the centrosome that likely relay cargo and signaling cues between this compartment and the broader cytoplasm. Known physical and functional interactions within these enriched proteins, such as the partnership of KIF3A with KIF3B in intraflagellar transport and the cooperation of CEP83 with FBF1 at distal appendages, illustrate how centrosomal submodules could collectively modulate intestinal epithelial responses in the setting of inflammatory bowel disease, even though their co-localization does not by itself prove a single shared pathogenic mechanism.

paragraphs: 20 submitted inflammatory bowel disease-associated proteins were significantly enriched in recycling endosome (GO:0055037).

Among the proteins enriched in this pathway, OPTN and RAB11A are notable because they link recycling endosome localization to vesicle trafficking events that are central to epithelial homeostasis. OPTN functions as an adaptor at endomembrane compartments, where it couples selected cargo and membranes to downstream processes such as vesicle sorting and degradation, and its enrichment in the recycling endosome suggests that a subset of inflammatory bowel disease–associated OPTN molecules operates at this tubular network. RAB11A is a small GTPase that regulates recycling endosome traffic toward the plasma membrane, particularly for receptors and adhesion molecules, so its presence in this compartment is consistent with a role in routing surface proteins that are important for intestinal barrier integrity and immune signaling. The attached literature on E-cadherin recycling highlights that recycling endosomes can determine junctional stability, and the enrichment of RAB11A within this compartment provides a plausible cellular context in which inflammatory bowel disease–associated variants might influence epithelial junctional dynamics, even though this analysis itself does not test that mechanism.

VPS52 stands out among the enriched proteins as a core component of the a non-intersection pathway component tethering complex that operates at the interface between recycling endosomes and the trans‑Golgi network, where it captures incoming vesicles and helps specify their fusion. Its enrichment in the recycling endosome indicates that a fraction of the inflammatory bowel disease–associated VPS52 pool resides on, or cycles through, this compartment, positioning it to influence the fidelity of receptor and transporter recycling back toward biosynthetic pathways. GRIA1, in contrast, exemplifies a cargo protein that depends on recycling endosome trafficking for its surface expression: as an ionotropic glutamate receptor subunit, its presence in this compartment points to regulated retrieval and re‑delivery of signaling receptors, which in the intestinal mucosa could affect neuronal or immune communication with the inflamed tissue, although this pathway analysis alone does not establish a specific signaling mechanism.

The remaining enriched proteins can be organized into functional clusters that share roles within the recycling endosome but may participate in distinct molecular processes. A first cluster comprises RAB10, RAB11B, RAB13, RAB35, RAB4A and RAB8A, which together represent a cohort of small GTPases that control different aspects of recycling endosome membrane dynamics, including vesicle budding, cargo sorting and targeted delivery to defined plasma membrane domains. A second cluster contains the syntaxin family members STX6, STX7, STX8 and STX12, which act as a non-intersection pathway component proteins that mediate vesicle docking and fusion events required for efficient export from, and trafficking through, the recycling endosome. A third cluster is formed by ANK2, TUBA1A, TUBG1 and TUBGCP4, which contribute structural and organizational functions, with ANK2 serving as a membrane–cytoskeleton linker and the tubulin components providing the microtubule scaffold and nucleation machinery that position and support the tubular recycling endosome network within the cell. Finally, VPS51 and VPS53, together with VPS52, represent the remaining subunits of the a non-intersection pathway component tethering complex, and their enrichment in this compartment underscores that long‑range vesicle tethering and endosome–Golgi connectivity are common features of the inflammatory bowel disease–associated proteome intersecting with the recycling endosome.

Overall, the enrichment of these proteins in the recycling endosome indicates that a substantial fraction of the inflammatory bowel disease–associated proteome localizes to, or transits through, a tubular endosomal network that controls the return of receptors, transporters and adhesion molecules to the plasma membrane. GO Cellular Component enrichment demonstrates co‑localization of these proteins in the recycling endosome but does not, on its own, prove that they act through a single shared mechanism in disease. Within this compartment, OPTN, RAB11A and VPS52 appear to be key drivers of the association, as they occupy nodal positions in cargo selection, vesicle trafficking and tethering at the recycling endosome interface. Well‑documented interactions among VPS51, VPS52 and VPS53 as components of the a non-intersection pathway component complex, and their functional cooperation with syntaxins such as STX6 during vesicle tethering and fusion, further support the idea that coordinated yet mechanistically diverse trafficking events at the recycling endosome form an important cellular context for inflammatory bowel disease–related pathology, including processes that impinge on epithelial barrier integrity and receptor recycling highlighted by studies of E‑cadherin trafficking.

Within the KEGG endocytosis map, the small GTPases RAB11A and RAB8A localize to the downstream recycling endosome branch, where they coordinate polarized trafficking back to the plasma membrane, and both have been implicated in the maintenance of the intestinal epithelial tight junction barrier that is characteristically impaired in inflammatory bowel disease. Experimental work on epithelial tight junction regulation and autophagy-dependent internalization of pore-forming claudins supports a role for RAB11A- and RAB8A-dependent recycling in controlling paracellular permeability, suggesting that their enrichment in endocytosis links this pathway to barrier failure in inflamed gut mucosa.

FOLR1 occupies a more upstream position in the pathway as a glycosylphosphatidylinositol-anchored folate receptor that is internalized via clathrin-dependent and -independent endocytosis, and altered folate handling has been reported in the intestinal mucosa of inflammatory bowel disease patients. By coupling ligand binding at the apical epithelial surface to endocytic uptake, FOLR1 provides a direct route by which changes in endocytic flux can influence folate-dependent epithelial metabolism and repair responses in the chronically inflamed intestine.

The a non-intersection pathway component regulators ARF1, ARF3, ARF4, ARF5, ARFGAP1, ARFGAP2, ARFGAP3 and the guanine nucleotide exchange factor GBF1 cluster in the KEGG map at the level of coat recruitment and vesicle budding from early endosomes and the Golgi, forming a relatively contiguous block along this branch of the pathway. CAPZA1, CAPZA2, CAPZA3 and CAPZB form an actin-capping complex that stabilizes filament barbed ends at endocytic sites, linking vesicle formation to cytoskeletal dynamics, while the microtubule-based motors KIF5A and KIF5B drive long-range movement of endocytic vesicles toward the perinuclear region, together providing the structural support required for efficient epithelial endocytic trafficking in the inflamed gut.

Taken together, the enrichment of these 21 proteins in KEGG:04144 indicates that the endocytic branch encompassing a non-intersection pathway component–GBF1–a non-intersection pathway component–driven vesicle budding and RAB11A/RAB8A-guided recycling is a prominent contributor to inflammatory bowel disease pathophysiology, particularly at the level of epithelial barrier control and cargo-specific uptake such as folate via FOLR1. The pattern of hits is concentrated along the vesicle formation and recycling arms of the pathway rather than scattered uniformly, with RAB11A, RAB8A and FOLR1 emerging as key drivers of the association. Well-documented interactions within the intersection, such as the activation of ARF1 by GBF1 and its inactivation by ARFGAP1–3, and the coupling of RAB11A-positive recycling endosomes to KIF5B-dependent transport, support a model in which coordinated regulation of vesicle budding, cytoskeletal attachment and recycling shapes the endocytic contribution to chronic intestinal inflammation.

paragraphs: 20 submitted inflammatory bowel disease-associated proteins were significantly enriched in a non-intersection pathway component interactions in vesicular transport (KEGG:04130).

Within the KEGG:04130 map, the proteins listed for this record cluster in the central vesicle fusion machinery rather than in upstream receptors or distal transcriptional outputs, occupying a near-contiguous block across the ER–Golgi and endosomal–phagosomal branches. SEC22B is a v-a non-intersection pathway component positioned on ER-derived vesicles that fuse with phagosomal or endosomal membranes, and experimental work on dendritic cells has shown that SEC22B-dependent ER–phagosome transport supports noncanonical cross-presentation to prime T cells, directly linking this enriched vesicular module to antigen handling processes that are relevant to intestinal immune activation in inflammatory bowel disease. In the same pathway segment, STX11 and STX4 act as target-membrane SNAREs at the plasma membrane and secretory granules in immune cells, where their established roles in regulated exocytosis and cytotoxic granule or cytokine release provide a mechanistic route by which altered a non-intersection pathway component interactions could modulate effector responses in the inflamed gut mucosa identified in inflammatory bowel disease cohorts.

SNAP29, STX17 and STX18 localize to the branch of the KEGG map that connects late endosomes and lysosomes to autophagosomes, placing these proteins at the interface between degradative trafficking and antigen presentation. STX17 is a well-characterized autophagosomal syntaxin that pairs with SNAP29 to drive autophagosome–lysosome fusion, and the identification of both proteins within the inflammatory bowel disease gene set supports the view that defective autophagic flux and cargo degradation may contribute to disease-associated alterations in intracellular antigen processing. STX18, which participates in ER–Golgi and early secretory pathway a non-intersection pathway component complexes within the same KEGG branch, provides an additional link between biosynthetic trafficking and the autophagy–lysosome system, suggesting that the disease-enriched module perturbs the continuity of membrane flow from the ER through to degradative compartments that ultimately shape mucosal immune presentation.

Other vesicle fusion proteins in this pathway reinforce the prominence of immune cell trafficking steps in the inflammatory bowel disease module. VAMP5, a vesicle-associated v-a non-intersection pathway component, and YKT6, a prenylated a non-intersection pathway component cycling between Golgi, endosomes and the plasma membrane, are positioned in KEGG:04130 at sites where secretory and recycling vesicles fuse with target membranes, indicating that vesicle delivery to the cell surface and to endosomal compartments is a recurrent theme among the enriched proteins. VTI1A, which partners with late endosomal and lysosomal syntaxins in the map, occupies a complementary position to VAMP5 and YKT6 on the luminal side of degradative trafficking, together highlighting that both sides of the a non-intersection pathway component pairing required for successful vesicle docking and fusion are represented in the inflammatory bowel disease–enriched gene set.

The remaining proteins are most readily understood as three functional clusters within the KEGG a non-intersection pathway component framework. An ER–Golgi trafficking cluster (BET1, BET1L, GOSR1, GOSR2, STX5, USE1, BNIP1, STX18, YKT6) spans the anterograde and retrograde routes between the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus, indicating that the core secretory pathway supplying membrane and cargo to the entire vesicular system is selectively enriched in the inflammatory bowel disease module. A second cluster of endosomal and lysosomal fusion SNAREs (STX6, STX7, STX8, VTI1A, VAMP5, STX16) maps to the late endosome–lysosome continuum and recycling endosomes, suggesting that sorting, degradation and recycling of receptors and cargo are jointly affected. Finally, an immune secretory a non-intersection pathway component cluster (STX4, STX11) sits at the plasma membrane branch where cytotoxic granules and secretory vesicles fuse with the cell surface, underlining the contribution of regulated exocytosis to the vesicular processes highlighted in inflammatory bowel disease.

Taken together, enrichment of these vesicle fusion factors in the a non-intersection pathway component interactions in vesicular transport pathway suggests that inflammatory bowel disease involves coordinated perturbation of the downstream effector layer of membrane trafficking that links the ER–Golgi system to endosomes, lysosomes and the plasma membrane. The association appears to be driven in particular by SEC22B, SNAP29 and STX17, which occupy nodal positions at the crossroads of ER–phagosome transport, autophagosome–lysosome fusion and antigen cross-presentation, and which also provide documented cross-talk to adjacent KEGG maps such as Antigen processing and presentation, Phagosome and Autophagy. Well-characterized a non-intersection pathway component complexes such as the STX17–SNAP29 pairing on autophagosomes and the BET1–STX5 partnership in ER–Golgi transport exemplify direct physical interactions among the proteins listed for this record that could integrate secretory, degradative and immunological vesicle traffic in the intestinal mucosa. In this context, the present pathway points to dysregulated a non-intersection pathway component-mediated vesicular fusion as a plausible unifying mechanism by which diverse cellular compartments contribute to chronic intestinal inflammation in inflammatory bowel disease.

paragraphs: 8 submitted inflammatory bowel disease-associated proteins were significantly enriched in Phagosome (KEGG:04145).

Within the directed KEGG phagosome map, RAB7B and STX7 localize to the late phagosome–lysosome fusion segment, downstream of particle uptake and early signaling. RAB7B functions as a small GTPase that regulates late endocytic and phagosomal trafficking, and its enrichment here in IBD mucosal tissue links altered control of phagosome maturation to the disease-associated transcriptomic module highlighted by integrative analyses. STX7 is a vesicle-associated a non-intersection pathway component that mediates fusion of late endosomes and lysosomes with maturing phagosomes; its presence among the enriched proteins in inflamed gut samples suggests that the membrane-remodeling steps required for degradative phagosome formation are specifically represented in the IBD-associated phagosome signature identified in spatial and bulk transcriptomic studies of active ileal Crohn’s disease.

SEC22B and STX18 occupy an intermediate position on the KEGG phagosome map, at the interface between ER–Golgi trafficking and the delivery of membrane and cargo to nascent phagosomes, and participate in documented cross-talk with adjacent KEGG maps such as a non-intersection pathway component interactions in vesicular transport and Endocytosis. SEC22B is an ER-derived v-a non-intersection pathway component involved in vesicle docking and fusion, and its enrichment in inflamed intestinal tissue indicates that ER-originating membrane traffic into the phagosomal system contributes to the IBD-linked phagosome module captured in integrative pathway analyses. STX18 is a t-a non-intersection pathway component that partners with ER–Golgi a non-intersection pathway component complexes and thereby supports membrane provisioning and cargo flow toward the phagosome; its inclusion among the enriched proteins in IBD mucosa reinforces the idea that reprogrammed secretory and endocytic flux, rather than receptor-level engagement, underlies much of the disease-associated phagosomal remodeling.

The remaining enriched proteins partition into two functional clusters that further refine the position of the signal within the KEGG phagosome pathway. A first cluster comprises STX12, which participates in recycling endosome–phagosome fusion events and thus links the phagosome map to the Endocytosis pathway through a non-intersection pathway component-dependent membrane exchange; its placement indicates that the IBD-enriched module extends across multiple vesicle fusion nodes rather than a single branch. A second, structurally coherent cluster consists of TUBA1A, TUBA4A, and TUBB4A, which encode α- and β-tubulin isoforms that form microtubules essential for phagosome transport, positioning, and maturation, and that also connect the phagosome map to the broader KEGG Cytoskeleton regulation and Autophagy-related pathways through shared use of the microtubule network.

Overall, enrichment of these proteins in KEGG:04145 indicates that the IBD signal within the phagosome pathway is concentrated in the vesicle trafficking, fusion, and maturation segments rather than at upstream receptors, and that it spans a contiguous block along the late phagosome branch with extensions into ER–phagosome and endosome–phagosome interfaces. RAB7B, SEC22B, and STX7 appear to drive this association by anchoring key late trafficking and fusion steps that are repeatedly highlighted in transcriptome-wide IBD studies and in proteomic analyses of phagosomes. Documented interactions among the intersection proteins, particularly a non-intersection pathway component pairing between SEC22B and STX18 and cooperative action of RAB7B with the microtubule components TUBA1A, TUBA4A, and TUBB4A, underscore a coordinated disturbance of phagosome dynamics in IBD rather than isolated perturbation of single molecules.

paragraphs: 11 submitted inflammatory bowel disease-associated proteins were significantly enriched in Protein processing in endoplasmic reticulum (KEGG:04141).

Among the proteins enriched in this pathway, HSP90AA1 is a central chaperone component of the endoplasmic reticulum protein quality control module in the KEGG map, functioning at the interface between folding of nascent polypeptides and the initiation of endoplasmic reticulum stress–signalling cascades. The attached literature on endoplasmic reticulum stress–induced cell death and on the role of endoplasmic reticulum stress in intestinal barrier regulation and inflammatory bowel disease supports a model in which impaired chaperone capacity heightens unfolded protein burden, thereby amplifying stress responses that contribute to epithelial injury and chronic intestinal inflammation; in this context, enrichment of HSP90AA1 links the chaperone arm of protein processing directly to the inflammatory bowel disease gene set.

SAR1B and SEC24C occupy more distal positions on the KEGG map, at the transition from endoplasmic reticulum folding and quality control to cargo selection and vesicle budding in a non-intersection pathway component-mediated export. SAR1B initiates coat assembly at endoplasmic reticulum exit sites, while SEC24C participates in cargo recognition, and the literature connecting endoplasmic reticulum stress with maintenance of the intestinal mucus barrier and with protection from necroptosis-induced colitis underscores the relevance of this export step for trafficking of secreted barrier components. The enrichment of SAR1B and SEC24C therefore links inflammatory bowel disease risk to the efficiency with which properly folded proteins are packaged and dispatched from the endoplasmic reticulum, a critical determinant of whether stress resolves or progresses to epithelial damage and cell death in the gut.

LMAN1 and LMAN2 form a functionally coherent group on the KEGG pathway as luminal lectin cargo receptors that cycle between the endoplasmic reticulum and early secretory compartments to capture correctly folded glycoproteins for a non-intersection pathway component export. Positioned immediately upstream of the a non-intersection pathway component coat components, they represent the luminal counterpart of the cytosolic cargo-selection machinery, and their enrichment suggests that the inflammatory bowel disease gene set includes determinants of how efficiently barrier- and immune-relevant glycoproteins are triaged for exit versus retention during endoplasmic reticulum stress states described in the literature on inflammatory bowel disease and endoplasmic reticulum stress–driven barrier dysfunction.

The remaining enriched proteins cluster into three functional modules within the downstream arm of the KEGG map. First, SAR1A, SEC23A, SEC24A, SEC24B and SEC24D constitute a core “a non-intersection pathway component inner-coat and cargo-selection cluster,” jointly responsible for coupling GTP-dependent coat initiation to selection of export cargo once proteins have passed endoplasmic reticulum quality control. Second, SEC31A forms a “a non-intersection pathway component outer-coat cluster,” providing the scaffold that completes vesicle budding from endoplasmic reticulum exit sites, and thereby translating intracellular stress and folding status into the rate of anterograde transport. Third, LMAN1 and LMAN2 together form a “luminal cargo-receptor cluster,” acting at the glycoprotein interface of the pathway to ensure that only suitably processed substrates engage the a non-intersection pathway component machinery; taken together, these clusters emphasize that the inflammatory bowel disease–enriched proteins are concentrated on the contiguous branch of the KEGG map that governs the handover from folded cargo to transport vesicle formation, with documented cross-talk from these coat and cargo-receptor modules to adjacent KEGG secretory and vesicular transport maps.

Overall, enrichment of these 11 proteins in KEGG:04141 indicates that inflammatory bowel disease risk variants are concentrated in components that couple endoplasmic reticulum protein quality control to a non-intersection pathway component-mediated export, a nexus repeatedly implicated by the literature on endoplasmic reticulum stress, epithelial barrier integrity and inflammation. HSP90AA1, SAR1B and SEC24C appear to drive this association by anchoring, respectively, the chaperone, coat-initiation and cargo-selection segments of the pathway within the inflammatory bowel disease module. Consistent with their placement on the KEGG map, these proteins interact physically and functionally, with SAR1A and SAR1B recruiting SEC23A and a non-intersection pathway component family members, including SEC24C, into prebudding complexes, and with LMAN1 and LMAN2 delivering cargo into these sites for encapsulation by SEC31A-containing coats. This coordinated network suggests that genetically or functionally impaired endoplasmic reticulum processing and export can favor the unresolved stress responses and epithelial injury that contribute to inflammatory bowel disease pathogenesis as described in the attached endoplasmic reticulum stress literature.

paragraphs: 26 submitted inflammatory bowel disease-associated proteins were significantly enriched in Kinesins (REAC:R-HSA-983189).

Within the Reactome hierarchy, Kinesins (R-HSA-983189) is curated as a pathway-level event, and the proteins listed for this record are annotated predominantly as components of ATP-dependent motor complexes that move along microtubule substrates; in this context, kinesin heavy chains function as catalysts for microtubule-based motility, kinesin light chains and KIFAP3 act as components of these catalytic complexes, and tubulin subunits provide the structural substrates on which successive reaction steps of cargo binding, translocation and release occur, with complexes such as KIF5A–KLC1–KIFAP3 acting within single reaction steps and other kinesins (for example KIF1A or KIF3A–KIF3B–KIF3C assemblies) operating in parallel or successive steps within the same event chain.

Among the enriched proteins, KIF9 is particularly notable because its genomic locus is linked to long noncoding RNAs that have been directly implicated in inflammatory bowel disease: a non-intersection pathway component has been reported, together with a non-intersection pathway component and a non-intersection pathway component, as a novel IBD biomarker, and an independent study shows that a non-intersection pathway component promotes cell apoptosis in IBD by modulating a microRNA-148a-3p/suppressor of cytokine signaling axis, suggesting that transcriptional activity at the KIF9 locus can influence epithelial or immune cell survival in the inflamed intestine even though the specific contribution of the KIF9 motor protein itself to these processes has not yet been defined.

The remaining enriched proteins can be organized into functional clusters reflecting their roles within the Kinesins pathway. A first cluster comprises the conventional kinesin-1 motor machinery, including KIF5A and KIF5B together with the light chains KLC1, KLC2, KLC3 and KLC4 and the adaptor protein KIFAP3; in Reactome these proteins form heteromeric kinesin-1 complexes in which KIF5A or KIF5B provides the ATPase motor activity (catalyst) while the light chains and KIFAP3 serve as cargo-binding components within the same reaction step of microtubule-based transport. A second cluster contains KIF1A, KIF1B, KIF1C and KIF13B, kinesin family members that function as monomeric or dimeric motors specialized for cargo transport along microtubules; they act as catalytic subunits in distinct transport reactions that run in parallel to kinesin-1–mediated movement within the pathway. A third, mitosis- and cytoskeleton-focused cluster includes KIF18B, KIF20B, KIF22, KIF4B, KIFC1, KIF21A, KIF21B and KIF26A, which are annotated as motors or regulatory components involved in spindle dynamics, chromosome alignment or microtubule remodeling, thereby catalyzing or modulating successive steps of microtubule reorganization events captured under the Kinesins pathway. A fourth cluster is formed by KIF3A, KIF3B and KIF3C, which assemble into heterotrimeric kinesin-2 complexes that act as catalytic motors for anterograde transport along microtubules in a single reaction step shared by all three subunits. Finally, TUBA1A, TUBA4A and TUBB4A constitute a microtubule-structural cluster, providing the alpha- and beta-tubulin substrates upon which all of the kinesin complexes in this pathway exert their ATP-dependent motor activity.

Overall, enrichment of these 26 proteins in the Kinesins pathway indicates that microtubule-based motor function and its underlying track components constitute a coherent module contributing to inflammatory bowel disease biology, with transcriptional activity at the KIF9 locus emerging as the principal driver connecting this pathway to intestinal inflammation. Within this module, kinesin-1 complexes built from KIF5A or KIF5B together with KLC1–KLC4 and KIFAP3, kinesin-2 complexes containing KIF3A–KIF3B–KIF3C, and other family members such as KIF1A and KIF13B converge on shared microtubule substrates formed by TUBA1A, TUBA4A and TUBB4A, illustrating dense physical interactions among the enriched proteins. These established interactions between kinesin motors, their light chains, adaptor proteins and tubulin subunits provide a plausible structural and transport framework through which regulatory disturbances at the KIF9 locus, and potentially at other kinesin family genes, could influence cellular behavior in the inflamed gut, although direct mechanistic links beyond a non-intersection pathway component remain to be elucidated in IBD-specific studies.

paragraphs: 87 submitted inflammatory bowel disease-associated proteins were significantly enriched in Cilium Assembly (REAC:R-HSA-5617833).

In the Reactome ontology, Cilium Assembly (R-HSA-5617833) is curated as a pathway-level event whose immediate parent event is the higher-order pathway “Organelle biogenesis and maintenance.” Within this pathway, CEP290, CC2D2A and related transition zone components act as structural constituents of multi-protein complexes that establish the ciliary gate, rather than as classical soluble catalysts or substrates. CEP290 and CC2D2A participate in the same transition-zone assembly reactions together with other a non-intersection pathway component/a non-intersection pathway component module proteins, forming successive structural intermediates along the event chain that build the diffusion barrier at the base of the cilium; their enrichment here indicates that defects in this structural gating machinery form a central element of the inflammatory bowel disease module. KIF3A functions as the catalytic ATPase subunit of the kinesin-2 motor complex, acting as a catalyst that drives anterograde intraflagellar transport in reactions downstream of basal body and transition-zone formation, and its presence among the enriched proteins links inflammatory bowel disease genes to the motile component of cilium biogenesis rather than only to static scaffolds.

Several enriched proteins participate in the earliest centriole- and basal body–focused reaction steps of Cilium Assembly as structural components of centrosomal and distal appendage complexes. CEP152, CEP135, CEP192, CEP250, CEP57 and CEP63 act as scaffold proteins within centriole duplication and pericentriolar matrix–recruitment reactions, serving as non-catalytic components of multi-subunit complexes that nucleate and organize microtubules before ciliary docking. In Reactome, CDK5RAP2 and NEDD1 likewise function as components of γ-tubulin–recruiting complexes in successive reactions that expand the pericentriolar matrix, positioning the nascent basal body for subsequent cilium extension in the IBD gene set. CEP162, CEP164, CEP83, FBF1, CEP131, CEP89 and ODF2 are incorporated as structural components of distal appendage and subdistal appendage complexes at the mother centriole, working largely within the same reaction steps that tether the basal body to the plasma membrane and define the site of ciliogenesis; their enrichment suggests that inflammatory bowel disease–linked variants converge on these membrane-docking reactions.

A second group of notable proteins shapes axonemal microtubule dynamics and cargo movement along the cilium. KIF3B, KIF3C and KIFAP3 form non-catalytic and catalytic subunits of the same kinesin-2 motor complexes as KIF3A, acting within the same intraflagellar transport reaction steps to move structural and signaling cargoes along the growing axoneme. MAPRE1, CKAP5 and CLASP1 function as microtubule plus-end tracking and stabilization factors, incorporated as structural and regulatory components rather than as substrates or products, and act in successive reactions to promote microtubule growth from the basal body into the ciliary shaft. MARK4, NEK2 and NDE1 provide catalytic and structural regulation of centrosomal microtubules in upstream reactions that license or restrain ciliogenesis by phosphorylating or scaffolding microtubule-associated targets, thereby shaping the microtubule network on which the downstream kinesin-driven transport steps depend in the inflammatory bowel disease module.

The remaining enriched proteins fall into several functional clusters. A transition-zone and basal body scaffold cluster comprises AHI1, ALMS1, MKS1, B9D1, B9D2, NPHP1, NPHP4, C2CD3, CEP41 and NINL, which act predominantly as structural components of a non-intersection pathway component/a non-intersection pathway component and related complexes in successive reactions that seal the base of the cilium and couple the basal body to the axoneme. A centriole-capping and licensing cluster includes CCP110 and CEP97, which form a complex within the same reaction step at the distal end of centrioles to cap and transiently suppress ciliogenesis until upstream duplication and docking events are completed. A microtubule nucleation and amplification cluster is formed by HAUS1, HAUS2, HAUS3, HAUS4, HAUS5, HAUS6, HAUS7 and HAUS8, which assemble into the augmin complex as structural subunits within shared reaction steps that generate branched microtubules feeding into basal body and axonemal growth. A vesicle trafficking and regulatory cluster comprises ARF4 (re-encountered here in the context of directing cargo to the nascent cilium), GBF1 and AKAP9, which act as a catalytic small GTPase and non-catalytic scaffold regulators within successive membrane-trafficking and signaling reactions that deliver ciliary components to the site of assembly. Finally, CSNK1D and HSP90AA1 function as a catalytic kinase and a chaperone complex component, respectively, modulating the stability and activity of ciliary structural proteins across multiple reaction steps rather than serving as terminal substrates or products.

Altogether, enrichment of inflammatory bowel disease proteins in Reactome Cilium Assembly supports a model in which defects across basal body formation, transition-zone scaffolding, intraflagellar transport and associated regulatory reactions contribute to disease risk. The association appears to be driven particularly by core structural transition-zone genes such as CEP290 and CC2D2A and by the transport motor component KIF3A, which together span early gating and later cargo-moving steps in the pathway. Well-documented interactions among these proteins in Reactome include the CCP110–CEP97 centriolar cap complex, the multi-subunit kinesin-2 complexes containing KIF3A, KIF3B, KIF3C and KIFAP3, and the clustered a non-intersection pathway component/a non-intersection pathway component module interactions linking AHI1, MKS1, B9D1, B9D2, NPHP1, NPHP4 and CEP290 in successive transition-zone assembly reactions. These interconnected complexes indicate that the inflammatory bowel disease gene set is not randomly distributed across ciliary biology, but instead concentrates within the core structural and motor machinery that executes the Cilium Assembly pathway.
